sets.title: Too many croissants on Sundays
sets.transcript:
M: Morning. Before we open, have a look at this. It's the list of what we threw away last Sunday.
W: Wow. Eleven croissants and six muffins? That's a lot.
M: It is. That's about thirty dollars in the bin, and it's like that most Sundays.
W: I've been thinking about that, actually. What if we sold everything at half price after three o'clock?
M: I thought about that too. But the bakery across the road tried it last spring. The owner told me people stopped coming in the morning. They just waited for the cheap prices.
W: Oh. I didn't know that.
M: So my idea is simpler. We bake less. Twenty croissants a day instead of thirty.
W: The thing is, on Saturdays we already run out. I've been writing down when the last croissant goes, and for the past three Saturdays it's been before eleven.
M: Really? Before eleven?
W: Yeah. And people who come in for lunch get pretty annoyed when there's nothing left. Last week a man asked me twice if we had any hidden in the back.
M: Hmm. So Sundays need fewer and Saturdays need more.
W: Could the baker just make more when we're running low?
M: Only if she knows in time. She can't keep coming out of the kitchen to check the shelf.
W: I could tell her. I'm right here at the counter anyway.
M: Okay. Then twenty to start with, and you tell her when we're down to the last five. She needs about half an hour to bake a new tray.
W: That's fine. I'll keep writing down the times, too, so we can see if it's working.
M: Great. Let's start today. I'll go and tell her now, so she can get some extra dough ready. Could you put the chairs out front? We open in fifteen minutes.
W: Sure, I'll do it right away.

speakers.S: a teacher giving a short lecture to a high-school class

sets.title: The firewood price rule
sets.transcript:
Today we're going to take one decision and follow everything that came after it. About two hundred years ago, the river town of Lindmere had a terrible winter. The river froze early, the boats that usually brought firewood down from the hills couldn't get through, and the price of a bundle of wood more than doubled in a month. Poor families were burning their own chairs to stay warm.

So the town council did something that sounded kind. It passed a rule that no one in Lindmere could sell a bundle of firewood for more than four pennies, which was roughly the price before the river froze. The thinking was simple. If wood stays cheap, everyone can afford to heat their homes. I'm going to argue that this rule did more harm than good, and I want to show you why by following its effects one at a time.

The first effect came within a week. The sellers who brought wood into town by cart, over the hill road, found that the trip wasn't worth it anymore. The road was icy, the horses had to be fed, and at four pennies a bundle they lost money on every load. So most of them simply turned around and sold their wood in Mardale, the next town along, where there was no limit. Lindmere didn't get cheap wood. It got less wood.

The second effect was about quality. The sellers who did stay found other ways to protect themselves. Bundles got smaller. Then they got wetter. Sellers mixed in green wood, which means wood that's freshly cut. It smokes badly and gives off much less heat. Officially, the price was still four pennies, but a family now needed two of those bundles to get the warmth that one used to give.

The third effect is the one I find most troubling. There wasn't enough wood for everyone, so sellers had to decide who got it, and they didn't decide by need. They sold to their regular customers, to friends, to anyone who could offer something extra on the side, a sack of flour, say, or a favour. The families with nothing extra to offer, the very families the rule was written for, ended up at the back of the line.

Here's the interesting part. A town record from that February lists how many carts came in over the hill road each week. Before the rule, it was around thirty. Three weeks after it, only nine carts came in, far fewer than before. Then in March the council quietly dropped the limit, and within two weeks the number was back above twenty. Prices were high, yes, but there was wood to buy.

So was the council wrong to want to help? No. The goal was a good one. My point is that the tool didn't fit the goal. If the council had used the town's money to buy wood and hand it to the poorest families, the sellers would have kept coming, and the help would have gone where it was needed.

For Thursday, write one paragraph on this question. Who, if anyone, gained from the rule?
